Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for LLM pipelines that write OMIM-style phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited. It uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries with 2-12 references each (515 papers; 19% readable in full via open access, the rest abstract or title only), and one model (Claude Opus 5.5) for writing, auditing and judging. Only the generation strategy varies: direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons. The primary endpoint ('OMIM facts conveyed') splits OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs (as deposited in ClinVar) once into 6,652 fixed atomic facts. A model judge then marks each fact as present, partly present, absent or contradicted in the draft paragraphs that cite the paper. Main findings: (i) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries, +43.7 points, CI +38.3 to +49.1; Table 24). (ii) The agent and the evidence graph are within about 0.5 points of direct reading, and the case table trails by 1.9 points (CI -3.1 to -0.8, sign test p=0.071; Table 1). Which design is ahead depends on the entry subset and, for the case table, on extraction settings (Appendix F). (iii) On 38 held-out entries a 'completeness pass' adds 2.6 points but makes drafts about 33% longer (Sec. 4.3). (iv) A planted-error test shows the claim-level audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but cannot see added citations (because of best-verdict aggregation) or omissions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4). The paper is unusually explicit about which analyses were pre-specified and which were post hoc, about safety-filter attrition, and about the lack of any human validation.
Strengths: Clean within-paper manipulation of access (Sec. 4.1, Table 24, Fig. 2a). The same papers are given as full text or as abstracts to the same writer on the same entries and facts. This isolates the effect of access from the usual confounds of era and journal, and the effect is large and consistent (better on 45 of 46 entries, tied on 1).

Strong experimental hygiene for an LLM-pipeline comparison. One model, shared guards and a shared audit for every strategy (Sec. 3.2, Table 4). Facts are split once without sight of any draft (Sec. 3.3). Paired bootstrap intervals and sign tests per entry, with Holm adjustment on the secondary measures (Table 8). Judge variation and run-to-run replicates give an explicit noise yardstick (Appendix E, Table 20). An intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis is included (Table 11), and the matched ablation separates settings from paradigm (Table 21).

Transparent status labelling. Section 3.3 lists every post hoc choice (a)-(i), including that the symmetric completion rule was adopted after a first analysis put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind (Appendix M.4). Tables 2-3 give the entry set, the comparison set and the reason for every dropout in every experiment. This is much better practice than is typical in the area.

Coverage is decomposed by whether the supplied text states each fact (Fig. 2b-c, Table 19, Fig. 6). This useful diagnostic shows that reading strategies convey 91-94% of stated facts and do no better than memory on facts the text does not state, so the remaining headroom for 'reading better' is small (about 4% of all facts; Sec. 4.1).

Safety-filter stops are treated as a measured outcome rather than silently retried (Sec. 3.3, Tables 5, 29, 55). The paper also shows that this choice can flip conclusions (Table 11; Table 32). This is a practical lesson for anyone benchmarking multi-call pipelines.

The audit stress test (Sec. 4.5, Tables 50-53) gives a concrete, mechanistically explained blind spot. Best-verdict aggregation over cited papers hides over-citation: 0 of 30 added citations were flagged, although the per-paper verdict was 'unsupported' for 176 of 176 claims. The test also states plainly that the audit checks fidelity, not correctness or completeness.

The memory-only control by creation era and on entries created in 2026 (Fig. 5, Tables 15-16, Appendix M.2) is a sensible, if partial, contamination check. It shows that memory-only coverage collapses to 5.7-7.0% on the newest entries while direct reading holds near 52%.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Fact splitting, fact-presence judging, the 'stated in the supplied text' labels and the audit verdicts are all made by the same model family that writes the drafts (Sec. 3.2; limitation (i) in Sec. 5). The 95.7% agreement between two judgings (Appendix E) shows only self-consistency. For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark and a measurement, a stratified expert check of even a few hundred fact judgements is missing. It would need chance-corrected agreement and particular attention to 'partly present' and 'not stated'. Without it, the absolute levels and the stated/not-stated decomposition cannot be fully trusted. The same applies to the small strategy differences (0.5-2 points) the paper interprets, which are the size where correlated judge errors and self-preference matter most.

The reference measures a narrow slice of the task. Strategies write whole phenotype entries, but the primary endpoint scores only OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs from gene entries (Sec. 3.1), because the phenotype narratives are not public. Only 327 of 515 papers have an in-scope paragraph (Sec. 3.1). About 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference (Appendix H). Synopsis F1 is about 35% for every reading strategy (Table 6), partly because 1,835 of the 2,311 HPO annotations come from HPO's own curation rather than OMIM. The title and abstract describe this as scoring knowledge-base entries, but most draft content is assessed only by the same-model audit.

Ceiling effects limit the main comparison. On stated facts, all reading strategies convey 91-94% (Table 19). On stated facts from abstract-only papers they reach about 96-97%, and most entries tie (Table 19, 79 entries, roughly 46-59 ties). By the paper's own count the headroom for reading better is about 4% of facts (Sec. 4.1). The null-to-small strategy differences therefore partly reflect a regime with 2-12 references and mostly abstracts, which the paper concedes 'favours direct reading' (Sec. 5). The regime where designs might separate (many relevant papers) could not be compared because of stopped replies (Sec. 4.4, Appendix K.2). The answer to 'how much does the strategy matter?' is thus restricted to an easy regime. The abstract's 'differ ... by a few points either way' should carry that restriction.

There is no formal equivalence analysis. The paper rightly declines to claim equivalence because no margin was set (Sec. 4.2). Even so, the central message that designs 'differ by a few points either way' is informal. A TOST against a margin justified by curation needs, or by the replicate-noise yardstick of ±1.0 point, would make the claim testable. As it stands, the CIs for the agent and the graph (-1.3 to 0.0; -1.5 to +0.5) exclude neither a small deficit nor a small advantage.

Conclusions about paradigms rest on one implementation each, and those implementations are sensitive to settings and to the entry set. Matched settings move the case table by +2.1 points (Table 21). The evidence graph's sign flips between the ablation's two halves (-1.2 vs +3.1 on the same drafts; Appendix F). It is ahead in all three replicates on the 30-entry subset but -0.5 on the full 93 entries (Appendix E). Statements of the form 'extract-then-write' versus 'read-and-write' are therefore about these prompts and settings, not paradigms, as the paper partly acknowledges (limitation iii).

The reading-better gains are confounded with length. The completeness pass lengthens drafts from 10,802 to 14,412 characters, and the merge adds 3.1 points partly on facts the text does not state, with more unsupported claims and lower variant precision (Sec. 4.3, Tables 30, 33, 34). The endpoint is recall-only with no precision or length counterpart (Sec. 3.3, limitation iv). The only precision-side check covers 20 entries with no interval (Table 33). A length-matched baseline would test whether +2.6 points exceeds what writing more yields: direct reading told to write about 14k characters, or a second unrevised sample of matched length. A coverage-per-length or precision-penalised endpoint would also help. Without one of these, 'reading more completely recovers a few points' is not separated from 'writing more recovers a few points'.

Safety-filter attrition is large, uneven and correlated with content, which makes the comparisons depend on completion. 7 of 100 main entries are dropped (Table 5). On the 2026 entries 10 of 30 are dropped, including 6 agentic-curator drafts (Table 55). Every large entry has at least one strategy stopped (Table 49), and STORM had 30 of 30 research prompts stopped (Table 37). The three entries the completeness pass lost are exactly the three where the evidence graph lost a paper (Appendix I), so stops track entry content. Comparing only completed entries conditions on a post-treatment outcome. Under ITT the agent's sign flips (+0.4 vs -0.6) and the case-table interval includes zero (Table 11). With a lost entry counted as zero, the completeness arms fall below baseline on the mean (-3.5, -4.8; Table 32). The adopted fallback (keep the unrevised draft) is a reasonable design decision. It is still a design choice and should not be read as a measured property of the arm.

The analysis has many forking paths. Nine post hoc choices are listed (Sec. 3.3 (a)-(i)). Two of them apply to every result: fixed fact lists replacing per-draft splitting, and the symmetric completion rule adopted after an unfavourable first result (Appendix M.4). The disclosure is commendable. However, pre-specification is not externally verifiable (no registration or time-stamped protocol is cited), and the main strategies were developed on their own evaluation entries (limitation ix). Only the 2026 entries (20 compared) and the reading-better split are held out.

The benchmark cannot be reused as released. The fixed fact lists contain curator wording and are not redistributed. A new user must rebuild the reference under the rights holder's terms and split it again, and the effect of a fresh split on levels was not measured (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; limitation v). The model ran through a CLI with no temperature or seed control (Appendix B). Contribution (1), a benchmark harness, therefore yields comparable numbers only within one split made by one team. Others cannot score a new strategy against the reported baselines.

The audit stress test is small and selected, as the paper notes. It uses 30 items per class, planted only in evidence-graph paragraphs that had already passed the audit, and the controls are paragraphs that passed once (Sec. 4.5, Appendix L), so no specificity estimate for arbitrary paragraphs is available. The paper identifies the best-verdict design flaw but does not evaluate the obvious alternative (flag when any cited paper fails), even though per-(claim, paper) verdicts exist for 78-88% of entries (Table 53). Those data could estimate the alternative rule's flag rate at no cost.

The comparisons with released pipelines add little. They cover 10 and 4 entries. PaperQA2 ran without its agent, STORM produced no article, and the protocol (six concatenated QA answers) differs from the strategies' one-pass entry writing (Appendix J, Tables 35-43). The statement that the study's own implementations 'are thus not outperformed by released pipelines' (Appendix J) is stronger than this design supports. The paper does flag the comparison as exploratory.

The main-text summary of the padding experiment is selective. Section 4.4 reports that padding 'cost no strategy more than about a point' in absolute terms. It does not mention that, relative to direct reading, the other strategies fell behind by 2.8-4.6 points at about 500k characters, with intervals excluding zero (Table 46, interaction). Nor does it mention that under the symmetric rule only 2 entries remain (Table 47).

Presentation is very dense. The 10-page body packs many numbers, entry counts and caveats into nearly every sentence (e.g., Secs. 1, 4.2, 4.3). Terms such as 'like for like', 'stopped reply', 'completion' and 'reading strategies' carry precise local meanings. The 44-page appendix of tables is hard to navigate. The paper contains no worked example of a curator paragraph, its fact list, a draft paragraph and the judge's and audit's verdicts, and no prompts appear in the paper. Such an example would greatly help readers judge construct validity and what 'partly present' means in practice.
Questions: Can you provide even a small expert validation of fact judgements and stated/not-stated labels (e.g., 200-300 facts stratified by access level and status) with chance-corrected agreement? The most decision-relevant targets are the facts where strategies disagree and the 'partly present' class.

How sensitive are the main strategy differences to a judge from a different model family? Re-judging the 93 entries' drafts against the same fixed fact lists would need no new generation and would directly test self-preference.

For the completeness pass, what happens with a length-matched control, e.g., direct reading instructed to write a draft of about 14,000 characters, or a second direct-reading sample appended without merging? What is the gain in coverage per 1,000 characters for each arm?

Using the per-(claim, paper) verdicts already recovered for Table 53, how many claims in real drafts would an 'any cited paper fails' rule flag, and how many of those are true over-citations on a small manual check?
Did you consider a pre-registered equivalence margin for the main comparison? With the existing data, what would a TOST at ±2 points conclude for the agent and the evidence graph?

What does the 0.5 weight on 'partly present' do to the strategy differences? The 'fully' row in Table 6 keeps the order of levels. Are the paired differences and CIs in Table 1 also stable under full credit only?
How much does a fresh split of the curator paragraphs by the same procedure move levels and paired differences? Two independent splits of a subset would quantify the reuse problem stated in Sec. 3.1.

Of the 111 (evidence graph) and 130 (case table) generated variants that OMIM does not list (Table 10), what share does the audit find supported by the cited papers? This would distinguish genuine extra recall from error in the 'variant precision' metric.

Given that the stopped replies concentrate on certain entries (Appendix I), can you characterise those entries (topic, paper content, length) to assess whether the completed-entry comparison is biased toward particular disorder types?

GraphRAG global search conveys 20.5% of facts the text does not state on 4 entries, against 3.0% for direct reading (Table 36). Is this an artefact of the looser community-report citation mapping or recalled content, and does it affect how 'not stated' coverage should be interpreted?
Limitations: The authors list limitations thoroughly (Sec. 5 (i)-(xii), the ethics statement): no human validation, one model family, a regime dominated by few references, a recall-only endpoint, a narrow and non-redistributable reference, open-access text without supplements, and the audit's blind spots. These are adequately disclosed. The main remaining gap is that some headline phrasings (abstract; Sec. 1 'designs differ by a few points either way') are not consistently tied to the regime of 2-12 references, mostly abstracts, and one model.
The reference covers only the variant-centred part of an entry, so conclusions about writing full knowledge-base entries extend beyond what the primary endpoint measures.

The safety filter of the single model shaped which entries and systems could be compared, including all large entries and STORM. Results may not transfer to other models or to the many-reference regime.
Released drafts are machine-generated text about genetic disorders. The paper states that they are not clinical guidance and must not be presented as OMIM content, which is appropriate.
